title: Deep Q-Network Candidate Restriction and Acuity Leakage in Privacy-Aware Healthcare IoT Task Offloading
content: Wearables in Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) networks offload tasks to edge, fog and cloud nodes, and a passive observer sees the destinations even when payloads are encrypted. Privacy-aware schedulers often penalise the entropy of that sequence, but whether lower entropy makes patient acuity harder to infer is rarely tested. We study DQN-ES, a scheduler in which a deep Q-network (DQN) restricts each decision to its top-K destinations and an exhaustive enumeration over the K-candidate set minimises a cost whose energy, latency and entropy weights depend on a criticality index. In a simulated four-tier network with 30 paired replicates, we compared it with the per-task optimum, random candidate restriction, entropy-reweighted greedy scheduling and a criticality-agnostic static rule, and trained an adaptive adversary to infer high acuity from each policy's flow metadata. In a secondary analysis across 21 policies, the entropy-based routing-predictability risk did not rank adversary AUC (Spearman rho = -0.065, p = 0.78). Raising the entropy weight lowered that risk from 0.41 to 0.14 while AUC rose from 0.60 to 0.73, because criticality-dependent weights separated acuity tiers by destination. DQN-ES leaked less than the per-task optimum (AUC 0.569 vs 0.612) at a cost of 13.7 ms, 14.6 mJ and 0.65 percentage points of deadline violations, and less than reweighted greedy at matched latency, where it leaked about as much as random restriction. Fully random restriction leaked less at 36.3 ms (95% CI 26.8 to 46.5) more latency, and the static rule least (AUC 0.483) at 55.6 ms more. Routing entropy measures routing predictability, not acuity leakage.
